title: Insured, but Still on the Hook: Who Bears the Most Risk in Homeowner's Insurance? - Liberty Street Economics
gist: NY Fed research estimates moral hazard in homeowner's insurance is cheap for insurers to manage, but contract terms leave households exposed to 29% of expected losses, concentrated among low-FICO households and high tail-risk properties.

insights.claim: Deductibles and coverage limits leave US homeowners exposed to an estimated 29% of expected losses even though the direct estimated cost of moral hazard to insurers is small.
insights.speaker: Hyeyoon Jung
insights.so_what: Insured does not mean protected; disaster losses spill onto household balance sheets and potentially mortgage credit.

insights.claim: Insurers keep moral hazard cheap by shifting risk to households via deductibles and limits, so the cost of incentive preservation shows up as retained household risk rather than insurer cost.
insights.speaker: Hyeyoon Jung
insights.so_what: Pricing and product design push tail risk onto households.

insights.claim: Lower-FICO households are estimated to be more risk averse, pay higher risk premia, face higher moral-hazard costs and retain more uninsured exposure, so those least able to absorb a disaster loss are the most exposed (correlational, not causal).
insights.speaker: Hyeyoon Jung
insights.so_what: Disaster shocks hit weaker borrowers hardest, relevant to mortgage credit risk.

insights.claim: Residual exposure is higher for properties facing greater tail disaster risk, with substantial geographic variation across counties.
insights.speaker: Hyeyoon Jung
insights.so_what: Geography determines where uninsured loss risk concentrates.

insights.claim: More financially constrained insurers (lower risk-based capital ratios) insure riskier properties and collect higher dollar premiums, but risk premium as a share of premium is flat, so higher premiums reflect risk matching, not higher margins.
insights.speaker: Hyeyoon Jung
insights.so_what: Insurer capital strength shapes which risks they hold.

insights.claim: The moral-hazard estimates behave as expected: costs are lower for homeowners with lower loan-to-value ratios and in states with inspection or verification requirements, and results hold when flood exposure is excluded.
insights.speaker: Hyeyoon Jung
insights.so_what: Supports model credibility; regulation can lower moral hazard.

insights.claim: A companion post will test what happens if insurers must offer full insurance, since the same contract features that expose households also preserve incentives to protect property.
insights.speaker: Hyeyoon Jung
entities: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
insights.so_what: Policy debate on mandated coverage upcoming.

top_entities: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
